rv.q: Yes, it really is that good. Since People, Places and Things premiered at the National Theatre in September, it’s become a bit of a juggernaut, racking up the awards nominations and glowing reviews. In these situations there’s always the danger of expectations being unreasonably inflated. But on a second viewing, if anything, it’s richer.

The play’s most audacious trick is that it does not pretend that there aren’t some serious upsides to hedonism. If you’ve heard one thing about the production, then it’ll almost certainly have been the performance of Denise Gough. To give Macmillan his well-deserved due, the role he has created is a humdinger.

Gough’s face is a remarkable battleground for Emma’s weapons-grade cynicism clashing with her desperate desire to make everything all right again. It is a titanic performance in a slightly flawed play. The only other cast member who can hold a candle to Gough is Marten, partly because she’s the only other one with a decent role.
